subject: History of USA
title: 7. Industrialization and Emergence as a World Power (1870–1916)

segments.text: Domestic industrial transformation and America’s larger overseas role developed together — economic power at home directly enabled greater strategic reach abroad, and a strong answer links the two rather than treating them as separate stories.

blocks.text: Industrial Growth and Its Social Costs

segments.text: Railroads linked national markets while steel, oil, electricity and machinery supported mass production; large corporations and new financial institutions accumulated unprecedented economic power. Industrial workers faced long hours, dangerous conditions and unstable employment, with unions such as the Knights of Labor and American Federation of Labor organising strikes and collective bargaining with mixed success. Millions of immigrants expanded the labour force and transformed urban culture, while rapid city growth produced serious housing, sanitation and political-machine problems alongside genuine new opportunity. Do not separate industrial growth from labour conflict and reform politics.
Do not call the Spanish-American War only a war to liberate Cuba; it also produced U.S. territorial expansion.
Do not assume economic growth benefited all groups equally.
A national railroad network and mass production created powerful corporations alongside harsh labour conditions.
The Spanish-American War (1898) resulted in U.S. control of Puerto Rico and the Philippines.
The Panama Canal opened in 1914, greatly increasing U.S. strategic and commercial reach.
Link domestic industrial power with expanding overseas strategic reach explicitly — they developed together, not as separate narratives.
Populist and labour movements are a direct political response to the same industrial transformation, not a separate topic.
